name: Backends for Frontends
intent: Give each kind of client its own small backend that shapes and combines data from shared services in the way that client needs.
scenario: A shop has a phone app and a website. Both show an order, but the phone needs two fields on a small screen and the site needs the customer, the lines and the total.
problem: Both clients call one general-purpose API. It returns every order field for everyone, so the phone downloads data it never shows, while the site still makes extra calls to other services, such as customers, to build one page. Every change to the API must be agreed with all clients.
solution: Each client gets its own backend (a BFF), owned by the team that builds that client. The mobile BFF calls the order service and returns only id and total. The web BFF calls the order and customer services and returns the full picture. The BFFs shape and combine data, and the shared services below them keep the business rules.
pain: The phone downloads fields it never shows
The website makes several calls to build one page
Changing the shared API means negotiating with every client
The one API is shaped by the loudest client
benefits: Each client receives exactly the data it needs
One request per screen, because the BFF combines the calls
The client team changes its own backend without waiting for others
Client-specific logic stays out of the shared services
whenToUse: Clients differ a lot in their needs: phone, web, TV, partner
Different teams own different clients and want to move at their own speed
Screens need data from several services combined
whenNotToUse: Clients with nearly identical needs: one API is simpler
A small team that cannot afford one more backend per client
When a GraphQL gateway already lets each client ask for exactly the fields it needs
pitfalls: Business rules copied into every BFF drift apart: keep rules in the shared services
BFFs multiply: each new client means a new service to run, secure and monitor
A BFF owned by a different team than its client brings the old coordination problem back
A BFF that grows rules and storage of its own becomes a second, hidden application

roles.label: Client
roles.description: A phone app, a website or another front end. It makes one request per screen to its own BFF.

roles.label: Backend for frontend
roles.description: A small backend for one client. It calls services, combines their answers and returns the shape that client needs.

roles.label: Shared service
roles.description: A domain service such as orders or customers. It holds the business rules and knows nothing about clients.

quiz.question: The phone app downloads a 200 KB order response, but its small screen shows only the order number and total. The website needs everything in it. What is the best fix?
options: Compress the response, so that the phone downloads the same data in fewer bytes
Cache the response on the phone, so that it downloads the order only once
Remove most fields from the shared API, and let the website make extra calls
Give the phone its own backend, which returns only the fields the phone shows
quiz.explanation: The phone should not receive data it never uses. A backend for the phone shapes the response for it, while the website keeps its own. Compression and caching still move the unused data, and trimming the shared API makes the website worse.

quiz.question: A company builds a BFF for each of six clients. Soon the discount calculation exists in all six, with small differences, and customers see different prices on different devices. What is the best fix?
options: Merge the six BFFs into a single backend, so that only one discount calculation exists
Keep business rules such as discounts in the shared services, and let BFFs only shape and combine data
Ask each client team to review the other teams' discount code every month for differences
Move the discount calculation into every client app, so that each client controls its own prices
quiz.explanation: A BFF should adapt data for its client. Rules that must be the same everywhere belong in the shared service the BFFs call. One merged backend loses the benefit, and monthly reviews or client-side rules keep several copies.

quiz.question: A shop has one website and one mobile app that need almost the same data, and a team of four. Someone proposes a separate BFF for each. What is the best response?
options: A single general API is simpler here, since the clients barely differ and the team is small
A BFF per client is always better, so build both and add a third for future clients
Build one BFF, but make the website and the app both call it with different keys
Build the BFFs, but put them in the clients so that no extra service has to run
quiz.explanation: A BFF earns its cost when clients differ and teams want independence. With near-identical needs and a small team, an extra backend per client is overhead. One BFF shared by two clients is just the general API again, and BFFs inside the clients are not backends.
